title: Arrival-pattern-sensitive batcher lab notes
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note collects exploratory runs and heuristics for making the continuous-batcher robust to non-stationary arrival patterns (bursty, diurnal, and multimodal) while preserving tail latency SLOs and inter-tenant fairness. Focus knobs: max_batch_size, dynamic_timeout_ms, urgency_decay, prefill_threshold, jitter_seed, and demotion_policy.

Context / problem statement:
- We’ve observed p95/p99 spikes when short bursts of high QPS hit machines with heterogeneous token-length distributions. Existing timeout-first flush + greedy fill causes either: (a) inflated small-batch penalty (too many small batches) or (b) long waits when waiting to fill for throughput.
- Goal: reduce p99 by ~20% on production-like replay while keeping throughput within 5% of baseline and avoiding starved low-priority tenants.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Seeding small randomized jitter on timeouts dampens synchronization and reduces multiple concurrent incomplete batches (empirical).
2) A two-tier timeout (soft_timeout + hard_timeout) with soft demotion yields better p95/p99 tradeoffs than single timeout.
3) Prefill borrowing (allowing a small budget of queued tokens to prefill new microbatches) improves latency for heterogeneous-length requests.

Experiment matrix (runs):
- Workloads: production-replay-A (mid QPS, mixed lengths), microburst-10s (sudden 10s spike), diurnal-shift (QPS ramp over 30m).
- Knobs: max_batch_size = {8, 16, 32}; soft_timeout_ms = {4, 8, 16}; hard_timeout_ms = {40, 80}; jitter_seed = {0, 1, 5} ms; prefill_threshold = {0%, 10%, 25%} (percent of batch token capacity).
- Fairness tests: two-tenant mixed (low priority background + high priority interactive).

Instrumentation and traces captured:
- Per-request microtrace (enqueue_time, batch_start, model_dispatch_start, first_byte, last_byte).
- Queue occupancy histogram per 100ms window.
- Batch composition logs (num_requests, token_sum, per-tenant shares).
- Tail sampler: randomly capture ~0.1% of p99 offenders with full trace and stack.

Key findings (summary):
- Jitter_seed=1-5ms reduced synchronized flush events by ~62% in microburst-10s (measured as simultaneous flushes within 2ms window). This correlated with p99 improvement ≈ 8-12ms on short-request-heavy traffic.
- Two-tier timeouts (soft=8ms, hard=80ms) combined with gentle demotion (urgency_decay=0.6 over 200ms) reduced p99 by 18% on production-replay-A compared to baseline single timeout=40ms, while throughput dropped <2%.
- Prefill_threshold=10% led to the best reduction of small-batch penalty for heterogeneous token distributions: p95 reduced by 6ms, p99 by ~10ms. Setting prefill too high (25%) created head-of-line effects for long requests (latency increase for long tails).
- Fairness: introducing a soft per-tenant reservation (2 requests worth) prevented background tenant starvation; without reservation, low-priority tenant queues experienced >3x latency during bursts.

Representative numbers (production-replay-A baseline -> tuned):
- Baseline (max_batch_size=32, timeout=40ms): p50=12ms, p95=38ms, p99=112ms, throughput=100k tokens/s
- Tuned (max_batch_size=16, soft=8ms/hard=80ms, jitter=3ms, prefill=10%): p50=11ms, p95=32ms, p99=92ms, throughput=98.5k tokens/s

Microtrace example (short request offender pre-tuning):
- enqueue -> wait 36ms -> dispatch -> first_byte 6ms -> last_byte 18ms => total ~60ms (in this case the wait dominated). After tuning, the same request waited only 9ms.

Interpretation and heuristics distilled:
- Small positive jitter on soft timeout is cheap and effective to break pathological synchronization (recommended default: 2-4ms seeded per-thread).
- Soft/hard timeouts allow preserving throughput by only hard-flushing very stale requests; tune soft to target p95 and hard to bound p99. Suggested starting ratio soft:hard = 1:10.
- Prefill helps when request token length variance is high; keep conservative (<=15%) to avoid head-of-line.
- For multi-tenant fairness, maintain a tiny per-tenant soft-reservation and a demotion window rather than hard deprioritization; this reduces starvation cascades without harming SLOs for interactive tenants.

Risks and failure modes:
- Aggressive jitter + tiny soft timeouts can increase CPU wakeups and overhead; monitor CPU and context-switch rate.
- Large prefill allows greedy tenants to monopolize batch capacity; enforce per-tenant caps.
- Incorrectly tuned demotion can produce oscillation where demoted requests flood at demotion expiry; add dampening.

Next steps / actionable items:
- (PR) Implement jitter_seed as per-thread rng seeded from steady clock: PR #1382 in review (linked above) — owner: Daniel.
- (Experiment) Run 7-day production A/B with tuned profile on 10% of serving machines; collect user-level p99 and cost delta. Owner: Sara.
- (Alert) Add telemetry for concurrent-flush-events metric and CPU wakeup counters. Owner: Priya.
- (Playbook) Draft an ops runbook for rollback when tuned profile increases long-tail for long requests. Owner: Omar.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Does soft/hard ratio need to vary by model family (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder)? early sims show decoder-only more sensitive to prefill.
- How does quantization-induced kernel variance interact with small-batch penalties? need kernel-level traces.

Notes to self / rough ideas: 
- Consider arrival-pattern classifier that switches batcher profile (aggressive small-batch) when we detect bursty arrivals vs steady state. Keep classifier simple (EWMA of inter-arrival variance).
- Explore combining prefill with KV-cache-friendly grouping so requests likely to hit similar KV keys are batched together.

Appendix: run checklist for reproducibility:
1) Checkout serving-runtime@exp/batcher-arrival-sensitivity
2) Load replay: production-replay-A (s3://replays/2025-08/prod-A)
3) Set knobs: see experiment matrix above; seed jitter with deterministic RNG for runs tagged "compare"
4) Collect metrics: p50/95/99 lat, batch size histogram, token throughput, per-tenant latency.
5) Archive sample microtraces under s3://traces/batcher/arrival-sensitivity/{run-id}

References and related notes:
- See linked Confluence page for historical runs and plots.
- PR #1120 contained earlier prefill experiment notes (we reused some scripts).

Quick verdict: the combo of small jitter + two-tier timeouts + conservative prefill + micro-reservations for tenants appears the most promising immediate tuning. Roll to canary, watch p99 and CPU churn.

-- end --
